nodes.paper_title: Mind Individual Information! Principal Graph Learning for Multimedia Recommendation
nodes.method_md:
# PGL To better capture local structural features,we propose the principal graph learning framework for multimedia recommendation. It first extracts the principal subgraph from the complete user-item interaction graph,and then employs message passing on the principal subgraph.The framework of PGL is illustrated in Figure 4. # Embedding As with many works (Zhou and Shen 2023; Yu et al. 2023c), we map the user unique hot ID representations to the user ID embeddings as the user raw representations.For the items, we map the content features using MLP to a low dimensional representation and concatenate them to obtain the item raw representations.Because the item content features are more informative than the item ID representations, it is more conducive to the model convergence. # Principal Graph Learning To better mine local structural features, we propose the principal user-item graph learning. Specifically, during model training，we first extract the principal subgraph from the complete graph structure.We then perform message passing on this principal subgraph.This approach not only mines richer individual information,but also captures cooccurrence patterns through multi-hop message passing. During model inference, we employ the message passing mechanism on the original complete graph instead, avoiding the problem of insufficient global information utilization caused by subgraph fragmentation. Formally, the message passing of $x$ is represented as: $$ \tilde { x } = H ( F ( \tilde { \mathbf { A } } ) ) x . $$ ![](images/216d4a68e13db886fe0d9d00d329b431ef17c81e992cc70a0efc6e6dbe5709c0.jpg) Figure 4: Comparison of (b) the proposed framework PGL and (a) exsiting framework LATTICE. For subgraph extraction $F ( \cdot )$ ， we design two operators: global-aware and local-aware subgraph extraction. The idea is to extract the most informative subgraph from the global/local perspective. · Global-Aware Extraction Truncated reconstruction $\tilde { \mathbf { A } }$ identifies the principal subgraphs with the highest information content, guided by the global structural signal. Specifically, we first decompose $\tilde { \mathbf { A } }$ using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) (Rangarajan 2Oo1). However, performing the exact SVD on $\tilde { \mathbf { A } }$ is computationally expensive,making it impractical in real-world scenarios.Instead,we adopt the randomized SVD algorithm proposed by (Halko,Martinsson,and Tropp 2O11). It approximates the range of the input matrix with a low-rank orthonormal matrix,and performs SVD on this smaller matrix. It is formally represented as: $$ \dot { \mathbf { U } } , \dot { \mathbf { A } } , \dot { \mathbf { U } } ^ { \top } = \operatorname { A p p r o x } { \mathbf { S } } \mathbf { V } \mathbf { D } ( \tilde { \mathbf { A } } , d ) , $$ where $\dot { \pmb { \Lambda } }$ is eigenvalues matrix, $\dot { \mathbf { U } }$ is corresponding eigenvector matrix, and $d$ is the rank of decomposed matrix.It is equal to the dimension of user/item raw representations. Next,we employ the truncated reconstruction to obtain principal subgraph $\dot { \bf A }$ ： $$ \begin{array} { r } { \ddot { { \mathbf U } } , \ddot { { \mathbf A } } , \dot { { \mathbf U } } ^ { \top } = \operatorname { T r u n c a t i o n } ( \dot { { \mathbf U } } , \dot { { \mathbf A } } , \dot { { \mathbf U } } ^ { \top } , \gamma ) , } \\ { \dot { { \mathbf A } } = \ddot { { \mathbf U } } \ddot { { \mathbf A } } \ddot { { \mathbf U } } ^ { \top } , \qquad } \\ { \ddot { { \mathbf A } } = { \mathrm { S p a r s i f i c a t i o n } ( \dot { { \mathbf A } } , \epsilon ) } , } \end{array} $$ where $\gamma$ is the truncation ratio within the range $( 0 , 1 )$ The truncation function retains the eigenvalues belonging to the range before or after $\gamma d$ ，resulting in $\ddot { \textbf { A } } =$ $\mathrm { D i a g } ( \lambda _ { 1 } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \lambda _ { \gamma d } , 0 , \cdot \cdot \cdot , 0 , \lambda _ { ( 1 - \gamma ) d } , \cdot \cdot \cdot , \lambda _ { d } )$ . The sparsification function sets elements with reconstruction values less than the threshold $\epsilon$ (typically $1 e ^ { - 3 }$ ）to O, ensuring the obtained principal graph $\dot { \bf A }$ remains sparse. · Local-Aware Extraction The expressive principal subgraph can also be extracted from the complete graph by leveraging local exposure information. The extraction process is formalized as: $$ \ddot { \mathbf { A } } = \mathrm { E x t r a c t i o n } ( \tilde { \mathbf { A } } , p ) . $$ Here, the extraction function is a multinomial samplig procedure, where $p$ denotes the percentage of original edges. Experiments finds that most of the time, $p = 0 . 3$ achieves an optimal result. The probability of sampling an edge connecting user $u$ and item $i$ is $1 / \sqrt { | \mathcal { N } _ { u } | } \sqrt { | \mathcal { N } _ { j } | }$ . This weighting scheme is motivated on the intuition that edges connected to nodes with lower exposure tend to be more reliable and informative (Wu et al. 2021). # Latent Graph Learning Following (Zhang et al. 2021; Zhou and Shen 2023; Yu et al. 2023c), we also conduct message passing on the latent itemitems to capture collaborative signals under modality information. Specifically, we first pre-construct latent item-item graphs based on similarity of item raw modality features $e _ { i , m }$ . It avoids the learning of latent graph structures in the classical LATTICE. Then, we use $k \mathbf { N N }$ sparsization $( k { = } 1 0 )$ and Laplacian regularization to obtain the normalized matrix $\mathbf { S } _ { m }$ . Besides, each modality item-item matrices are weighted added to obtain the final item-item similarity matrix S.Here, we still use the message passing mechanism of Equation 8. # Prediction To make recommendations for user $u$ ,we predict the interaction scores between the user $u$ and all candidate items, and choose $K$ top-ranked items as recommendations to the user $u$ .The interaction score is calculated as: $$ \begin{array} { r } { \begin{array} { c } { f _ { \mathrm { p r e d i c t } } ( u , i ) = \hat { \mathbf { e } } _ { u } ^ { \intercal } \hat { \mathbf { e } } _ { i } , } \\ { \hat { \mathbf { e } } _ { u } = \mathbf { e } _ { u } ^ { \mathrm { p r i n c i p a l } } + \mathbf { e } _ { u } ^ { \mathrm { l a t e n t } } , \hat { \mathbf { e } } _ { i } = \mathbf { e } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { p r i n c i p a l } } + \mathbf { e } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { l a t e n t } } , } \end{array} } \end{array} $$ where $\mathbf { e } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { { p r i n c i p a l } } }$ and $\mathbf { e } _ { i } ^ { \mathrm { { l a t e n t } } }$ represent the output of principal graph learning and latent graph learning correspondingly. The best result is in boldface and the second best is underlined. high score suggests that the user $u$ is more likely to click the item $i$ # Optimization During the phase of model training,we adopt the Bayesian Personalized Ranking(BPR） loss $\mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { B P R } }$ as the basic optimization task,which assumes that users prefer historically interacted items over unclicked ones.And it is combined with auxiliary self-supervised tasks to jointly update the representations of users and items: $$ \begin{array} { r } { \mathcal { L } = \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { B P R } } + \lambda _ { \mathrm { S S L } } \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { S S L } } , } \end{array} $$ where $\lambda _ { \mathrm { S S L } }$ is the hyperparameter to control the intensity of the self-supervised auxiliary task. The self-supervised task is used to further enhance the distinguishability of representations. Specifically, it first masks certain node representations through feature masking,and then maximizes the consistency of features after two random masks through in batch InfoNCE: $$ \begin{array} { r l } & { { \hat { \bf e } } _ { u } ^ { \prime } , { \hat { \bf e } } _ { u } ^ { \prime \prime } = { \bf M a s k } ( { \hat { \bf e } } _ { u } , \rho ) , } \\ & { { \hat { \bf e } } _ { i } ^ { \prime } , { \hat { \bf e } } _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime } = { \bf M a s k } ( { \hat { \bf e } } _ { i } , \rho ) , } \\ & { \quad \mathcal { L } _ { \mathrm { S S L } } = \displaystyle \sum _ { u \in \mathcal { U } } - \log \frac { ( { \hat { \bf e } } _ { u } ^ { \prime } \cdot { \hat { \bf e } } _ { u } ^ { \prime \prime } / \tau ) } { \sum _ { v \in \mathcal { U } } \exp ( { \hat { \bf e } } _ { v } ^ { \prime } \cdot { \hat { \bf e } } _ { v } ^ { \prime } / \tau ) } } \\ & { \quad \quad \quad + \displaystyle \sum _ { i \in \mathcal { L } } - \log \frac { \exp ( { \hat { \bf e } } _ { i } ^ { \prime } \cdot { \hat { \bf e } } _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime } / \tau ) } { \sum _ { j \in \mathcal { L } } \exp ( { \hat { \bf e } } _ { j } ^ { \prime } \cdot { \hat { \bf e } } _ { i } ^ { \prime \prime } / \tau ) } , } \end{array} $$ where $\rho$ controls the feature masking ratio and $\tau$ is the temperature hyper-parameter of the softmax function.
nodes.idea: Existing GNN-based multimedia recommendation methods focus on global structural features (co-occurrence patterns) but underutilize local structural features (individual information), leading to overly similar user preferences. PGL addresses this by extracting a principal subgraph from the user-item interaction graph using global-aware and local-aware extraction operators. Message passing on this subgraph captures both co-occurrence patterns and individual information. A self-supervised task enhances discriminability of representations.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- γ (truncation ratio): Controls the truncation in global-aware extraction. Typical value: 0.25, range: (0,1)
- p (sampling ratio): Percentage of original edges in local-aware extraction. Typical value: 0.3
- λ_SSL (weight for SSL): Controls the intensity of the self-supervised loss. Searched in [0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5]
- ρ (feature masking ratio): Controls the masking in self-supervised task. Searched in [0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]
- τ (temperature): Temperature in the softmax for self-supervised task. Typical value: 0.2

# coding: utf-8
# @email: y463213402@gmail.com
r"""
PGL
################################################
Reference:
    https://github.com/demonph10/PGL
    AAAI'2025: [Mind Individual Information! Principal Graph Learning for Multimedia Recommendation]
"""

import os
import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

from common.abstract_recommender import GeneralRecommender
from sparsesvd import sparsesvd


class PGL(GeneralRecommender):
    def __init__(self, config, dataset):
        super(PGL, self).__init__(config, dataset)
        self.mode = config['mode']

        self.embedding_dim = config['embedding_size']
        self.feat_embed_dim = config['feat_embed_dim']
        self.knn_k = config['knn_k']
        self.lambda_coeff = config['lambda_coeff']
        self.n_layers = config['n_mm_layers']
        self.n_ui_layers = config['n_ui_layers']
        self.reg_weight = config['reg_weight']
        self.mm_image_weight = config['mm_image_weight']

        self.n_nodes = self.n_users + self.n_items

        self.sub_graph, self.mm_adj = None, None

        # load dataset info
        self.interaction_matrix = dataset.inter_matrix(form='coo').astype(np.float32)
        self.norm_adj = self.get_norm_adj_mat().to(self.device)
        self.edge_indices, self.edge_values = self.get_edge_info()
        self.edge_indices, self.edge_values = self.edge_indices.to(self.device), self.edge_values.to(self.device)
        self.edge_full_indices = torch.arange(self.edge_values.size(0)).to(self.device)

        self.user_text = nn.Embedding(self.n_users, self.embedding_dim)
        self.user_image = nn.Embedding(self.n_users, self.embedding_dim)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.user_image.weight)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.user_text.weight)

        dataset_path = os.path.abspath(config['data_path'] + config['dataset'])
        mm_adj_file = os.path.join(dataset_path,'mm_adj_freedomdsp_{}_{}.pt'.format(self.knn_k, int(10 * self.mm_image_weight)))

        if self.v_feat is not None:
            self.image_embedding = nn.Embedding.from_pretrained(self.v_feat, freeze=False)
            self.image_trs = nn.Linear(self.v_feat.shape[1], self.feat_embed_dim)
        if self.t_feat is not None:
            self.text_embedding = nn.Embedding.from_pretrained(self.t_feat, freeze=False)
            self.text_trs = nn.Linear(self.t_feat.shape[1], self.feat_embed_dim)

        if os.path.exists(mm_adj_file):
            self.mm_adj = torch.load(mm_adj_file)
        else:
            if self.v_feat is not None:
                indices, image_adj = self.get_knn_adj_mat(self.image_embedding.weight.detach())
                self.mm_adj = image_adj
            if self.t_feat is not None:
                indices, text_adj = self.get_knn_adj_mat(self.text_embedding.weight.detach())
                self.mm_adj = text_adj
            if self.v_feat is not None and self.t_feat is not None:
                self.mm_adj = self.mm_image_weight * image_adj + (1.0 - self.mm_image_weight) * text_adj
                del text_adj
                del image_adj
            torch.save(self.mm_adj, mm_adj_file)
        self.dropoutf = nn.Dropout(config['dropout'])

    def sparse_mx_to_torch_sparse_tensor(self, sparse_mx):
        """Convert a scipy sparse matrix to a torch sparse tensor."""
        sparse_mx = sparse_mx.tocoo().astype(np.float32)
        indices = torch.from_numpy(np.vstack((sparse_mx.row, sparse_mx.col)).astype(np.int64))
        values = torch.from_numpy(sparse_mx.data)
        shape = torch.Size(sparse_mx.shape)
        return torch.sparse.FloatTensor(indices, values, shape)

    def get_knn_adj_mat(self, mm_embeddings):
        context_norm = mm_embeddings.div(torch.norm(mm_embeddings, p=2, dim=-1, keepdim=True))
        sim = torch.mm(context_norm, context_norm.transpose(1, 0))
        _, knn_ind = torch.topk(sim, self.knn_k, dim=-1)
        adj_size = sim.size()
        del sim
        # construct sparse adj
        indices0 = torch.arange(knn_ind.shape[0]).to(self.device)
        indices0 = torch.unsqueeze(indices0, 1)
        indices0 = indices0.expand(-1, self.knn_k)
        indices = torch.stack((torch.flatten(indices0), torch.flatten(knn_ind)), 0)
        # norm
        return indices, self.compute_normalized_laplacian(indices, adj_size)

    def compute_normalized_laplacian(self, indices, adj_size):
        adj = torch.sparse.FloatTensor(indices, torch.ones_like(indices[0]), adj_size)
        row_sum = 1e-7 + torch.sparse.sum(adj, -1).to_dense()
        r_inv_sqrt = torch.pow(row_sum, -0.5)
        rows_inv_sqrt = r_inv_sqrt[indices[0]]
        cols_inv_sqrt = r_inv_sqrt[indices[1]]
        values = rows_inv_sqrt * cols_inv_sqrt
        return torch.sparse.FloatTensor(indices, values, adj_size)

    def get_norm_adj_mat(self):
        A = sp.dok_matrix((self.n_users + self.n_items,
                           self.n_users + self.n_items), dtype=np.float32)
        inter_M = self.interaction_matrix
        inter_M_t = self.interaction_matrix.transpose()
        data_dict = dict(zip(zip(inter_M.row, inter_M.col + self.n_users),
                             [1] * inter_M.nnz))
        data_dict.update(dict(zip(zip(inter_M_t.row + self.n_users, inter_M_t.col),
                                  [1] * inter_M_t.nnz)))
        A._update(data_dict)
        # norm adj matrix
        sumArr = (A > 0).sum(axis=1)
        # add epsilon to avoid Devide by zero Warning
        diag = np.array(sumArr.flatten())[0] + 1e-7
        diag = np.power(diag, -0.5)
        D = sp.diags(diag)
        L = D * A * D
        # covert norm_adj matrix to tensor
        L = sp.coo_matrix(L)
        row = L.row
        col = L.col
        i = torch.LongTensor(np.array([row, col]))
        data = torch.FloatTensor(L.data)
        if self.mode == 'global':
            self.sub_graph = self.global_subgraph_extraction(L)
            self.sub_graph = self.sparse_mx_to_torch_sparse_tensor(self.sub_graph).to(self.device)

        return torch.sparse.FloatTensor(i, data, torch.Size((self.n_nodes, self.n_nodes)))

    def global_subgraph_extraction(self, adj):
        norm_adj = adj.tocsc()
        ut, s, vt = sparsesvd(norm_adj, self.embedding_dim)

        # Get the top and bottom 25% of singular values
        num_top_bottom = int(0.25 * self.embedding_dim)
        top_singular_values = s[:num_top_bottom]
        bottom_singular_values = s[-num_top_bottom:]

        # Compute the product of the top and bottom singular values
        product_singular_values = top_singular_values * bottom_singular_values

        # Construct the sparse matrix from the product of singular values
        product_matrix = np.diag(product_singular_values)
        product_sparse_matrix = ut.T[:, :num_top_bottom] @ product_matrix @ vt[:num_top_bottom, :]
        product_sparse_matrix = sp.csr_matrix(product_sparse_matrix * (abs(product_sparse_matrix) >= 1e-3))
        return product_sparse_matrix

    def alignment(self, x, y):
        user, item = self.interaction_matrix.nonzero()
        x, y = F.normalize(x, dim=-1), F.normalize(y, dim=-1)
        return (x[user] - y[item]).norm(p=2, dim=1).pow(2).mean()

    def uniformity(self, x, t=2):
        x = F.normalize(x, dim=-1)
        return torch.pdist(x, p=2).pow(2).mul(-t).exp().mean().log()

    def save(self):
        pass

    def pre_epoch_processing(self):
        if self.mode == 'local':
            # degree-sensitive edge pruning
            degree_len = int(self.edge_values.size(0) * 0.3)
            degree_idx = torch.multinomial(self.edge_values, degree_len)
            # random sample
            keep_indices = self.edge_indices[:, degree_idx]
            # norm values
            keep_values = self._normalize_adj_m(keep_indices, torch.Size((self.n_users, self.n_items)))
            all_values = torch.cat((keep_values, keep_values))
            # update keep_indices to users/items+self.n_users
            keep_indices[1] += self.n_users
            all_indices = torch.cat((keep_indices, torch.flip(keep_indices, [0])), 1)
            self.sub_graph = torch.sparse.FloatTensor(all_indices, all_values, self.norm_adj.shape).to(self.device)

    def _normalize_adj_m(self, indices, adj_size):
        adj = torch.sparse.FloatTensor(indices, torch.ones_like(indices[0]), adj_size)
        row_sum = 1e-7 + torch.sparse.sum(adj, -1).to_dense()
        col_sum = 1e-7 + torch.sparse.sum(adj.t(), -1).to_dense()
        r_inv_sqrt = torch.pow(row_sum, -0.5)
        rows_inv_sqrt = r_inv_sqrt[indices[0]]
        c_inv_sqrt = torch.pow(col_sum, -0.5)
        cols_inv_sqrt = c_inv_sqrt[indices[1]]
        values = rows_inv_sqrt * cols_inv_sqrt
        return values

    def get_edge_info(self):
        rows = torch.from_numpy(self.interaction_matrix.row)
        cols = torch.from_numpy(self.interaction_matrix.col)
        edges = torch.stack([rows, cols]).type(torch.LongTensor)
        # edge normalized values
        values = self._normalize_adj_m(edges, torch.Size((self.n_users, self.n_items)))
        return edges, values

    def forward(self, adj):
        if self.v_feat is not None:
            image_feats = self.image_trs(self.image_embedding.weight)
        if self.t_feat is not None:
            text_feats = self.text_trs(self.text_embedding.weight)

        image_feats, text_feats = F.normalize(image_feats), F.normalize(text_feats)
        user_embeds = torch.cat([self.user_image.weight, self.user_text.weight], dim=1)
        item_embeds = torch.cat([image_feats, text_feats], dim=1)

        h = item_embeds
        for i in range(self.n_layers):
            h = torch.sparse.mm(self.mm_adj, h)

        ego_embeddings = torch.cat((user_embeds, item_embeds), dim=0)
        all_embeddings = [ego_embeddings]
        for i in range(self.n_ui_layers):
            side_embeddings = torch.sparse.mm(adj, ego_embeddings)
            ego_embeddings = side_embeddings
            all_embeddings += [ego_embeddings]
        all_embeddings = torch.stack(all_embeddings, dim=1)
        all_embeddings = all_embeddings.mean(dim=1, keepdim=False)
        u_g_embeddings, i_g_embeddings = torch.split(all_embeddings, [self.n_users, self.n_items], dim=0)
        return u_g_embeddings, i_g_embeddings + h

    def bpr_loss(self, users, pos_items, neg_items):
        pos_scores = torch.sum(torch.mul(users, pos_items), dim=1)
        neg_scores = torch.sum(torch.mul(users, neg_items), dim=1)

        maxi = F.logsigmoid(pos_scores - neg_scores)
        mf_loss = -torch.mean(maxi)

        return mf_loss

    def InfoNCE(self, view1, view2, temperature):
        view1, view2 = F.normalize(view1, dim=1), F.normalize(view2, dim=1)
        pos_score = (view1 * view2).sum(dim=-1)
        pos_score = torch.exp(pos_score / temperature)
        ttl_score = torch.matmul(view1, view2.transpose(0, 1))
        ttl_score = torch.exp(ttl_score / temperature).sum(dim=1)
        cl_loss = -torch.log(pos_score / ttl_score)
        return torch.mean(cl_loss)

    def calculate_loss(self, interaction):
        users = interaction[0]
        pos_items = interaction[1]
        neg_items = interaction[2]

        ua_embeddings, ia_embeddings = self.forward(self.sub_graph)

        u_g_embeddings = ua_embeddings[users]
        pos_i_g_embeddings = ia_embeddings[pos_items]
        neg_i_g_embeddings = ia_embeddings[neg_items]

        batch_mf_loss = self.bpr_loss(u_g_embeddings, pos_i_g_embeddings, neg_i_g_embeddings)
        cl_loss = (self.InfoNCE(self.dropoutf(u_g_embeddings), self.dropoutf(u_g_embeddings), 0.2)
                   + self.InfoNCE(self.dropoutf(pos_i_g_embeddings), self.dropoutf(pos_i_g_embeddings), 0.2)) / 2
        return batch_mf_loss + self.reg_weight * cl_loss

    def full_sort_predict(self, interaction):
        user = interaction[0]

        restore_user_e, restore_item_e = self.forward(self.norm_adj)
        u_embeddings = restore_user_e[user]

        # dot with all item embedding to accelerate
        scores = torch.matmul(u_embeddings, restore_item_e.transpose(0, 1))
        return scores

nodes.paper_title: LightGCN: Simplifying and Powering Graph Convolution Network for Recommendation
nodes.idea: LightGCN simplifies traditional graph convolutional models for collaborative filtering by removing feature transformation and nonlinear activation, keeping only neighborhood aggregation. The method propagates user and item embeddings through the interaction graph and combines embeddings from multiple layers via weighted summation. This lightweight design improves training stability, reduces unnecessary computation, and yields better recommendation accuracy by focusing solely on graph-based embedding smoothing.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- **embedding_size**: Dimensionality of user/item ID embeddings (e.g., 64).
- **n_layers**: Number of graph propagation layers (typically 1–4; 3 works well).
- **alpha_k**: Layer combination weights for each propagation layer, often set uniformly to 1/(K+1).
- **lr**: Learning rate for Adam optimizer (default 0.001).
- **lambda_reg**: L2 regularization coefficient on ID embeddings (tested in 1e-6 to 1e-2 range).
- **batch_size**: Mini-batch size for BPR training (e.g., 1024 or 2048).
- **neg_sampling_strategy**: Strategy for selecting negative items during BPR training (standard uniform negative sampling).

nodes.paper_title: Bootstrapping User and Item Representations for One-Class Collaborative Filtering
nodes.idea: BUIR addresses the one-class collaborative filtering problem where only positive implicit feedback is available and negative sampling becomes unreliable in sparse datasets. The key idea is to eliminate negative sampling entirely by using a bootstrapped two-encoder framework: an online encoder predicts target embeddings produced by a momentum-updated target encoder. This prevents representation collapse while learning user–item similarity purely from positive interactions. In addition, BUIR introduces stochastic neighbor-based data augmentation to generate multiple perturbed views of each interaction, improving robustness under extreme sparsity.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- **embedding_dim**: Dimensionality of user/item latent embeddings (commonly 50–250).
- **momentum_tau**: Momentum coefficient controlling the update speed of the target encoder (typical range 0.9–0.999; default ~0.995).
- **learning_rate**: Step size for optimizing the online encoder (e.g., 1e-3 to 1e-4).
- **weight_decay**: L2 regularization coefficient for encoder parameters (1e-1 to 1e-5 depending on dataset).
- **drop_prob_max**: Maximum random neighbor-drop probability used in data augmentation (0.0–1.0).
- **predictor_layers**: Number of layers in the prediction MLP (typically 1; deeper networks can degrade performance).
- **batch_size**: Size of minibatches used during training (varies by dataset size).

nodes.paper_title: Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering
nodes.idea: This paper introduces Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering (NGCF), a method that integrates user-item interactions into the embedding process using graph neural networks (GNNs). NGCF explicitly models high-order connectivity in user-item graphs by propagating embeddings through multiple layers. This allows for better capture of collaborative signals and the refinement of item and user embeddings. The key innovation of NGCF is the embedding propagation mechanism, which injects collaborative filtering signals into the learning process in an explicit way, improving the quality of embeddings and recommendation performance.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- Embedding size (d): The dimension of user and item embeddings, typically set to 64.
- Number of layers (L): Defines the depth of the embedding propagation. A common choice is 3 layers.
- Dropout ratio: The ratio of dropout applied to the nodes and messages in the propagation process, typically set between 0.0 and 0.8.
- Learning rate: The step size for model optimization, typically set from 0.0001 to 0.005.
- L2 regularization strength (λ): Controls the strength of the regularization, often tuned between {1e-6, 1e-5, ..., 1e-2}.

nodes.paper_title: M2GRL: A Multi-task Multi-view Graph Representation Learning Framework for Web-scale Recommender Systems
nodes.domain: Multi-view Graph Representation Learning for Recommendation
nodes.task: Multi-view Graph Representation Learning for Recommendation
nodes.idea: M2GRL targets web-scale recommendation with rich side information, where items have multiple views such as instance, category and shop sequences. Instead of fusing all side information into a single embedding, it constructs one graph per view and learns separate node representations on each graph using skip-gram with negative sampling. It then defines inter-view alignment tasks that map embeddings from different views into a relational space via linear transformations and optimize them to align linked nodes across views. All intra-view and inter-view tasks are trained jointly in a multi-task framework, where homoscedastic uncertainty is used to adaptively weight task losses, removing the need for manual loss-weight tuning. The resulting multiple embeddings can be used directly for candidate generation and can also be combined with downstream metric-learning models to support both accuracy-oriented and diversity-oriented recommendation in large-scale industrial systems. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
nodes.hyperparam_def: - embedding_dim: Dimension of node/item embeddings in each view; typically around 64 in the paper, balancing representation capacity and efficiency. - num_views: Number of single-view graphs constructed from behavior and side information (e.g., 3 on Taobao: instance, category, shop; 2 on MovieLens: instance, category). - window_size: Context window size c for the skip-gram objective when generating intra-view training pairs; usually set near 9 to capture local co-occurrence patterns while keeping training efficient. - num_negative_samples: Number of negative samples k per positive skip-gram pair; controls training speed and the strength of noise-contrastive learning signal, typically 7–10 (the paper uses 10). - batch_size: Number of training samples per update step; large batches such as 2048 are used to fully utilize distributed GPU/CPU resources in web-scale training. - learning_rate: Step size for Adam/SGD optimizers when updating embeddings and alignment matrices; set around 0.01 in the main experiments to ensure stable yet fast convergence. - num_epochs: Number of passes over the training data, usually about 10 for the large Taobao and MovieLens logs. - min_task_weight (or uncertainty clip): Lower bound (e.g., 0.05) applied when converting homoscedastic-uncertainty σ² into 1/σ² task weights so that no task dominates or vanishes during multi-task optimization.

nodes.paper_title: Latent Structure Mining with Contrastive Modality Fusion for Multimedia Recommendation
nodes.idea: MICRO targets multimedia recommendation where items have visual and textual content, and addresses two issues of prior work: (1) item–item relations from multimodal semantics are not explicitly modeled, and (2) multimodal fusion is coarse (global concatenation/weighting shared across all items). The method first constructs modality-aware kNN graphs from raw content features and then learns latent graph structures per modality with a skip connection to denoise and refine these graphs. Graph convolutions over these learned graphs inject modality-specific item–item affinities into item embeddings. An attention mechanism fuses the modality-specific item embeddings into a multimodal representation, while a contrastive InfoNCE loss maximizes agreement between each modality-specific embedding and the fused embedding so that the fused representation captures modality-invariant item relations. The final fused item representations are added on top of standard collaborative filtering backbones (e.g., MF, NGCF, LightGCN) as a plug-and-play module, improving ranking accuracy and alleviating item cold-start by propagating feedback over learned semantic graphs. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- **embedding_dim (d)**: Dimensionality of user/item ID and modality-aware embeddings; typically set to 64 to balance capacity and efficiency.
- **k (kNN neighbors)**: Number of nearest neighbors kept when building modality-specific item graphs from cosine similarities; the paper commonly uses k = 10, with performance peaking at small to medium values.
- **lambda (λ, skip-connection weight)**: Balances initial kNN graph and learned latent graph in A_m = λ S_m + (1−λ) A'_m; typically around 0.7 so that both raw and learned structures contribute while controlling noise.
- **num_layers (L)**: Number of GCN propagation layers on the modality-aware item graphs; searched in {0,1,2,3,4,5}, with best results often at L = 1 for Clothing and L = 2 for Sports/Baby before deeper layers introduce noise/over-smoothing.
- **tau (τ, temperature)**: Temperature parameter in the InfoNCE contrastive loss controlling sharpness of similarity distributions; set to about 0.5 in experiments.
- **beta (β, contrastive loss weight)**: Coefficient for the contrastive auxiliary loss in the total objective L = L_BPR + β L_C; tuned in a small range (e.g., 0.01–0.05) with a typical value β ≈ 0.03 to help the main recommendation task without dominating it.
- **learning_rate**: Step size for Adam optimizer over all parameters (graph-structure layers, GCN, fusion, and CF backbone); usually 5e-4.
- **weight_decay (L2 reg)**: ℓ2 regularization strength on model parameters; set around 1e-4 to prevent overfitting while preserving expressiveness.

nodes.paper_title: BPR: Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback
nodes.idea: BPR addresses item recommendation from implicit feedback (clicks, purchases, views) where only positive interactions are observed and standard MF/kNN training treats all missing entries as negatives. The paper proposes a generic Bayesian optimization criterion, BPR-Opt, for personalized ranking: from each user’s implicit history it constructs training triples (u, i, j) meaning that user u prefers observed item i over unobserved item j, models p(i >_u j | Θ) with a logistic function over the score difference x̂_ui − x̂_uj, and maximizes the summed log-sigmoid plus an L2 prior on parameters. This is equivalent to directly optimizing a smooth surrogate of AUC instead of rating reconstruction. A stochastic gradient descent algorithm, LearnBPR, samples triples uniformly with replacement to avoid skew and scale to O(|S|) updates. The framework is instantiated on matrix factorization and adaptive item-kNN, showing that re-training these models with BPR-Opt yields substantially better ranking (higher AUC) on real implicit-feedback datasets than SVD-based MF, weighted-regularized MF (WR-MF), cosine kNN, or popularity baselines.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- embedding_dim (k): Rank of the latent factorization for BPR-MF; controls the capacity of user/item embeddings. The paper varies k from about 8 up to 128 dimensions, with performance generally improving up to a moderate k before saturating.
- learning_rate (alpha): Step size for stochastic gradient descent in LearnBPR; too large causes divergence, while too small slows convergence. Typically chosen as a small positive value and tuned on validation data.
- regularization_strengths (λ_Θ, λ_W, λ_H+, λ_H−): L2 penalties on user factors, item factors for positive updates, and item factors for negative updates (and analogously for kNN similarities); prevent overfitting and balance how strongly parameters are pulled toward zero. Set to small values (e.g., 10^-4–10^-2) and tuned per dataset.
- num_updates (or epochs / m·|S| steps): Total number of SGD updates (triples sampled) used to train the model. The paper scales this linearly with the number of observed interactions |S| and stops when AUC on a validation split stabilizes.
- sampling_strategy: Defines how training triples (u, i, j) are drawn from DS. The default is uniform bootstrap sampling over users, positive items, and negatives; alternative biased samplers could emphasize popular or recent items.
- model_type (BPR-MF vs BPR-kNN): Chooses the underlying scoring model x̂_ui (matrix factorization or adaptive item-kNN). For BPR-kNN, the item–item similarity matrix C plays the role of parameters and has its own regularization strengths for positive vs. negative updates.
- kNN_scope (for BPR-kNN): For the adaptive kNN instantiation, controls whether all previously interacted items or only a subset (top-k neighbors) contribute to the prediction for a candidate item; affects both accuracy and computational cost.

nodes.paper_title: Revisiting Graph based Collaborative Filtering: A Linear Residual Graph Convolutional Network Approach
nodes.idea: LR-GCCF is a graph-based collaborative filtering model that simplifies GCN-style recommenders by removing nonlinear transformations and introducing residual preference learning across propagation layers. User–item interactions are modeled as a bipartite graph; node embeddings are updated via linear neighborhood aggregation (simple graph convolution) over multiple layers. Instead of only using the final-layer embeddings, LR-GCCF views each layer as learning a residual preference component and aggregates layer-wise user/item embeddings for prediction, which mitigates over-smoothing, eases optimization, scales better to large graphs, and improves recommendation accuracy over prior GCN-based CF methods.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- **Embedding dimension D**: Size of user and item latent vectors (e.g., 64); controls model capacity and memory.
- **Propagation depth K**: Number of linear graph convolution layers (e.g., 1–4; often 3–4 for Amazon Books, 3 for Gowalla); trades off higher-order signal capture vs. over-smoothing.
- **L2 regularization coefficient λ**: Weight on L2 penalty for embeddings to prevent overfitting (e.g., 0.0001–0.1; 0.01 works well in the paper).
- **Learning rate**: Step size for SGD/Adam updates (e.g., 0.0001–0.01); tuned to balance convergence speed and stability.
- **Batch size**: Number of sampled user–(positive, negative) triplets per update in BPR training (e.g., a few thousand; fixed across baselines in experiments).
- **Top-N depth N for evaluation**: Cutoff for HR@N and NDCG@N metrics (e.g., N ∈ {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}); not a training hyperparameter but important for model selection.

nodes.paper_title: Denoising Implicit Feedback for Recommendation
nodes.idea: The paper addresses the problem of noisy implicit feedback in recommendation systems, where false-positive interactions (e.g., clicks that do not reflect user satisfaction) mislead training. The key idea is that false-positive interactions typically have larger loss values in early training stages. Based on this, the proposed Adaptive Denoising Training (ADT) dynamically prunes large-loss interactions using two paradigms: Truncated Loss, which discards interactions above a dynamic threshold, and Reweighted Loss, which assigns lower weights to large-loss interactions. This helps in reducing the impact of noisy data without requiring additional feedback.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- ε_max: Maximum drop rate for Truncated Loss, controlling the proportion of interactions to discard. Typical values: 0.05, 0.1, 0.2.
- ε_N: Iteration number to reach maximum drop rate for Truncated Loss, adjusting the pace. Typical values: 1000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 30000.
- β: Weight parameter for Reweighted Loss, controlling the extent of down-weighting. Typical values: 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.

nodes.paper_title: Self-Guided Learning to Denoise for Robust Recommendation
nodes.idea: This paper proposes a new denoising paradigm, Self-Guided Denoising Learning (SGDL), which leverages the memorization effect of recommendation models during training. SGDL operates in two phases: the 'memorization' phase, where memorized interactions are collected and used as denoising signals, and the 'self-guided learning' phase, where these memorized samples guide the learning to avoid noisy feedback. SGDL adapts automatically to identify clean and informative samples, providing a robust solution to implicit feedback noise without the need for predefined weighting functions. The method is model-agnostic and can be applied to any recommendation model.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- learning_rate: Learning rate for training, typically ranges from 10^-4 to 10^-2.
- hidden_size: The size of hidden layers in the MLP and LSTM units used for adaptive denoising, usually set to 64.
- batch_size: The number of samples per training batch; values depend on the dataset, such as 128 for MovieLens.
- memorization_history_length: Number of previous epochs considered for defining memorization, typically chosen from {2, 5, 10, 20}.
- loss_function: The loss function used in the base recommendation model, such as Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE) or BPR (Bayesian Personalized Ranking).
- scheduler: Adaptive denoising scheduler, typically LSTM or MLP, with learning rates tuned independently.

nodes.paper_title: Frequency Spectrum is More Effective for Multimodal Representation and Fusion: A Multimodal Spectrum Rumor Detector
nodes.idea: This paper introduces FSRU, a novel approach for multimodal rumor detection that operates in the frequency domain. It leverages Fourier transforms to convert spatial features of text and images into the frequency spectrum, which provides a sparse and global representation. Key innovations include unimodal spectrum compression to extract discriminative features within each modality, cross-modal spectrum co-selection to emphasize informative components across modalities, and dual contrastive learning to enhance multimodal alignment. This method avoids the quadratic complexity of attention-based fusion and improves efficiency and performance by exploiting frequency domain properties.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- α: weight for fully-supervised intra-modal contrastive loss, typical value 0.2
- β: weight for self-supervised inter-modal contrastive loss, typical value 0.2
- k: number of filters in unimodal spectrum compression, typical value 2
- learning_rate: initial learning rate, dataset-dependent (e.g., 1e-2 for Weibo, 1e-5 for Twitter)
- batch_size: number of samples per batch, typical value 64
- num_epochs: number of training epochs, typical value 50
- embedding_dim: dimension of text and image embeddings, typical value 256

nodes.paper_title: Self-supervised Graph Learning for Recommendation
nodes.idea: SGL enhances graph-based collaborative filtering models by introducing a self-supervised contrastive learning task on the user-item interaction graph. It creates multiple graph views via node dropout, edge dropout, or random walk, and maximizes agreement between representations of the same node across views. This mitigates degree bias, improves robustness to noisy interactions, and accelerates convergence when combined with LightGCN.
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- **lambda_ssl (λ₁)**: Weight controlling the strength of the self-supervised loss; typical values {0.005, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5, 1.0}.
- **tau (τ)**: Temperature parameter in InfoNCE contrastive loss (0.1–1.0); lower τ emphasizes hard negatives.
- **rho (ρ)**: Dropout/masking ratio for augmentation operators (0–0.5), used for node dropout, edge dropout, or random walk.
- **embedding_size (d)**: Dimensionality of user/item embeddings; commonly 64 or 128.
- **n_layers**: Number of GCN propagation layers (1–3 in experiments).
- **lambda_reg (λ₂)**: Weight decay for L2-regularization applied to model parameters.

nodes.paper_title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
nodes.idea: Introduces the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) as a scalable latent-variable generative model trained by maximizing the ELBO with an amortized inference network. The key technical contribution is the SGVB estimator using the reparameterization trick to obtain low-variance, unbiased stochastic gradients, enabling end-to-end minibatch training of both encoder qφ(z|x) and decoder pθ(x|z).
nodes.hyperparam_def:
- Latent dimension (d_z): size of latent code z; typical 16–256.
- Likelihood family (pθ(x|z)): Bernoulli for binary data or Gaussian for continuous data; determines decoder output parameterization.
- Encoder/decoder architecture: number of layers and hidden units (e.g., 1–3 layers, 128–1024 hidden units).
- Minibatch size (M): samples per update; typical 64–512.
- Monte Carlo samples (L): samples from qφ(z|x) to estimate expectations; often 1.
- Optimizer & learning rate (lr): SGD/Adagrad/Adam; lr typically 1e-4–1e-2.
- Prior p(z): usually N(0, I) (fixed); implicitly sets latent regularization strength.
- KL weight (β): weight on KL term in ELBO (β=1 in standard VAE; sometimes tuned 0.1–5 for β-VAE variants).

nodes.paper_title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
nodes.idea: Proposes Graph Convolutional Networks for semi-supervised node classification by stacking simple message-passing layers that propagate and transform node features with a symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix. The key technical idea is a first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions plus a “renormalization trick” (add self-loops and normalize) to make propagation stable and scalable, yielding an efficient 2-layer model trained with cross-entropy on labeled nodes. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0} :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

edges.relation_text: Paper P (BM3) explicitly positions itself as an alternative to graph-based multimodal recommenders such as Paper Q (LATTICE), which learns modality-specific item–item graphs from visual/text features and injects these high-order item relations into CF backbones via GCN layers.  Concretely, P keeps the LightGCN-style user–item backbone and even borrows Q’s architectural trick of adding a residual connection from the initial item ID embeddings when aggregating GCN layers, but it removes Q’s auxiliary item–item graphs and BPR-based negative sampling.  Instead, P proposes a self-supervised bootstrap scheme that generates dropout-based latent views and optimizes a multi-modal contrastive loss (graph reconstruction + inter-/intra-modality alignment), thereby learning user/item representations using only the user–item graph. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2} In its theoretical complexity analysis and experiments, P treats Q as a key state-of-the-art baseline—deriving Q’s O(|I|³) item-graph construction cost and directly comparing accuracy, memory, and training time—arguing that P achieves better recommendation quality while avoiding Q’s expensive item–item graph learning.

Paper P (BM3) directly builds on Paper Q (LightGCN) by using LightGCN as its backbone encoder for user–item ID embeddings. Specifically, P adopts LightGCN’s simplified graph propagation layer and its layer-aggregation mechanism to encode structural information from the user–item interaction graph, and then extends Q by adding multi-modal feature projectors, latent-view dropout, and a multi-modal contrastive loss. Thus, P inherits Q’s lightweight graph convolution paradigm and integrates it into a self-supervised multi-modal recommendation framework.

Paper P (BM3) draws directly from Paper Q (BUIR) by adopting its bootstrapping-based self-supervised learning paradigm. Specifically, P simplifies and extends Q’s BYOL-style framework: Q uses two encoders (online/target) with momentum updates and contrastive losses without negative samples, while P removes the target encoder, keeps the predictor–stop-gradient mechanism, and repurposes Q’s bootstrap idea to generate latent contrastive views via dropout. P then generalizes Q’s one-class CF formulation to the multimodal recommendation setting by adding multi-modal projection modules and designing new inter- and intra-modality contrastive losses on top of Q’s bootstrap-style positive-only training strategy.

Paper P (Mining Latent Structures for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (Graph-Refined Convolutional Network for Multimedia Recommendation with Implicit Feedback) by introducing a new method for explicitly modeling item-item relationships, which are crucial for multimedia recommendation. While Paper Q focuses on refining interaction graphs to mitigate noisy, false-positive edges, Paper P extends this by integrating a modality-aware structure learning layer to capture latent item-item semantic relationships from multimodal features. Paper P improves upon Paper Q by enhancing the item representations through learned graphs that reflect these relationships and injecting them into collaborative filtering methods, thus addressing the gap in prior methods that mainly relied on user-item interactions. Additionally, Paper P employs graph convolutions on the learned item-item graphs, while Paper Q primarily focuses on graph refinement and pruning, making Paper P's approach more focused on discovering and utilizing fine-grained item relationships for more comprehensive recommendations.

Paper P (Mining Latent Structures for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (MMGCN: Multi-modal Graph Convolution Network for Personalized Recommendation of Micro-video) by introducing a novel method for modeling fine-grained item-item relationships based on multimodal content. Paper Q constructs modality-specific user-item bipartite graphs and uses graph convolutions to learn user preferences for each modality. Paper P extends this approach by incorporating a modality-aware structure learning layer to learn item-item relationships across multiple modalities. Unlike Paper Q, which directly uses raw multimodal features to inform user-item interactions, Paper P uses these features only to learn graph structures and performs graph convolutions on item ID embeddings to directly capture item-item affinities. This approach from Paper P helps overcome limitations in traditional methods by modeling the latent item relationships, enhancing recommendation performance.

Paper P (Mining Latent Structures for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (LightGCN: Simplifying and Powering Graph Convolution Network for Recommendation) by adopting the concept of leveraging graph convolution operations on user-item interaction graphs. Specifically, Paper P extends the idea of graph convolutions from Paper Q by incorporating multimodal features to construct modality-specific item graphs. Unlike LightGCN, which simplifies graph convolution by focusing on neighborhood aggregation, Paper P introduces a more complex model by fusing multiple modalities to enhance item representations. This results in the explicit modeling of latent item-item relationships, which are further refined through graph convolutions to improve recommendation accuracy. Paper P compares its method to LightGCN, demonstrating improvements in capturing the collaborative signal from multimodal features and extending the generalization capabilities of graph-based collaborative filtering models.

Paper P (Mining Latent Structures for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering) by integrating the concept of graph convolutions and high-order connectivity modeling. While Paper Q introduces the idea of using graph neural networks (GNNs) for collaborative filtering by propagating embeddings through user-item interaction graphs, Paper P extends this by incorporating multimodal features to enhance item-item relationships. Paper P introduces a modality-aware structure learning layer, which learns item graphs from multimodal data and performs graph convolutions on these latent item graphs. Unlike Paper Q, which uses graph convolutions on user-item interactions alone, Paper P utilizes multimodal features to discover latent semantic relationships between items, further improving recommendation accuracy. Thus, Paper P builds upon the graph-based methods in Paper Q, adding a multimodal perspective to explicitly model item relationships.

Paper P (Self-Supervised Learning for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (VBPR: Visual Bayesian Personalized Ranking from Implicit Feedback) by incorporating visual signals into the recommendation process. While Paper Q introduces the idea of integrating visual features into collaborative filtering for improving recommendation accuracy and addressing cold-start issues, Paper P extends this by introducing self-supervised learning (SSL) techniques to better exploit multi-modal data. Paper P applies self-supervised contrastive learning to multi-modal content, using data augmentation to enhance the representation learning process. Specifically, it uses the insights from VBPR about visual features and incorporates them into a broader SSL framework, helping the model uncover multi-modal patterns and generalize better to unseen or noisy data, which is a limitation in VBPR. Thus, Paper P extends Paper Q by using SSL to learn richer, more robust representations from multi-modal data, further improving recommendation performance.

Paper P (Self-Supervised Learning for Multimedia Recommendation) extends Paper Q (MMGCN: Multi-modal Graph Convolution Network for Personalized Recommendation of Micro-video) by incorporating self-supervised learning (SSL) into the recommendation process. While Paper Q focuses on using graph convolution networks (GCNs) to learn representations for users and micro-videos based on multi-modal content, Paper P improves this approach by introducing SSL tasks to uncover latent patterns across different modalities. Specifically, Paper P applies data augmentation strategies such as feature dropout, feature masking, and contrastive learning to learn richer and more robust representations from multi-modal data. This approach allows Paper P to better capture multi-modal patterns and improve recommendation performance compared to traditional supervised methods like MMGCN, which lacks SSL integration.

Paper P (Self-Supervised Learning for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (LightGCN: Simplifying and Powering Graph Convolution Network for Recommendation) by applying self-supervised learning (SSL) to enhance the performance of graph-based recommendation models. Paper Q introduces LightGCN, which simplifies the graph convolution operation for collaborative filtering by removing unnecessary components like feature transformation and non-linear activation. Paper P extends this work by incorporating SSL, using data augmentation and contrastive learning to uncover latent multi-modal patterns. Specifically, Paper P uses LightGCN as a backbone model and adds SSL tasks (like feature dropout and masking) to distill additional supervisory signals from unlabelled data. This results in better representations and improved recommendation accuracy, especially in cold-start scenarios and with sparse data, building on the graph-based approaches of LightGCN.

Paper P (Self-Supervised Learning for Multimedia Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering) by leveraging graph neural network (GNN) techniques for collaborative filtering in the context of multimedia recommendation. Paper Q introduces Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering (NGCF), which incorporates high-order connectivity in the user-item graph by recursively propagating embeddings, thus enhancing the collaborative signal in the embeddings. Paper P extends this approach by introducing self-supervised learning (SSL) into the process. Specifically, Paper P uses SSL to uncover multi-modal patterns in the data, improving the model's robustness and generalization ability. It employs SSL tasks, including feature dropout and masking, to generate multiple views of the data, which are then contrasted to enhance the embeddings further. Thus, Paper P builds upon NGCF’s graph-based embedding propagation by adding self-supervised tasks to exploit hidden patterns in multi-modal data.

Paper P (A Tale of Two Graphs: Freezing and Denoising Graph Structures for Multimodal Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (Mining Latent Structures for Multimedia Recommendation) by refining the graph structure learning process for multimodal recommendation. Paper Q introduces the concept of learning latent item-item structures from multimodal features through graph convolutions. In contrast, Paper P critiques the inefficiency of this approach and proposes a simpler, more efficient method by freezing the item-item graph structure and denoising the user-item interaction graph. While Paper Q dynamically learns item-item graphs and fuses multimodal graphs to incorporate high-order relationships, Paper P suggests that the item-item graph from multimodal features can be precomputed and frozen, avoiding the overhead of learning these structures during training. Thus, Paper P directly builds on the architecture of Paper Q, simplifying it by freezing the graph structures while maintaining competitive performance in multimodal recommendation tasks.

Paper P (A Tale of Two Graphs: Freezing and Denoising Graph Structures for Multimodal Recommendation) builds on Paper Q (Self-Supervised Learning for Multimedia Recommendation) by extending the use of graph-based models in multimodal recommendation systems. Paper Q introduces the use of self-supervised learning (SSL) to uncover multi-modal patterns and improve the robustness of multimedia recommendation systems, while Paper P builds upon this idea by focusing on the graph structure learning aspect. Specifically, Paper P uses a graph convolutional network (GCN) backbone, similar to Paper Q’s approach, but introduces the concept of 'freezing' the item-item graph and 'denoising' the user-item interaction graph. By doing so, Paper P simplifies the graph structure learning process, improving computational efficiency and memory cost, while still leveraging SSL tasks to enhance the representation learning from multimodal data. In essence, Paper P builds upon the multi-task learning framework and SSL techniques from Paper Q to create a more efficient graph-based recommendation model.

Paper P (FREEDOM) builds on Paper Q (LightGCN) by simplifying and improving its graph structure learning approach. FREEDOM borrows from LightGCN's foundational use of graph convolution for recommendation, but it modifies this approach by freezing the item-item graph and applying a denoising method to the user-item graph. Specifically, while LightGCN uses dynamic graph learning for user-item interactions and item-item relations, FREEDOM freezes the item-item graph (constructed from raw multimodal features) and denoises the user-item graph to eliminate noisy interactions. This results in a more efficient model that significantly reduces computational cost while improving recommendation accuracy. Thus, FREEDOM extends LightGCN by simplifying the graph learning process and providing better scalability and performance under large datasets.

Paper P (FREEDOM) builds on Paper Q (NGCF) by incorporating some of its key ideas while introducing new innovations. NGCF utilizes graph neural networks to propagate user and item embeddings across the user-item interaction graph, refining them through embedding propagation layers. Paper P (FREEDOM) extends this approach by explicitly freezing the item-item graph structure and denoising the user-item graph, which results in improved efficiency and reduced computational cost compared to NGCF. While NGCF leverages high-order connectivity in the graph for collaborative filtering, FREEDOM optimizes this by freezing the item-item graph and denoising the user-item interaction graph. Thus, FREEDOM uses the collaborative signal propagation mechanism of NGCF but improves upon it by simplifying the graph learning process, demonstrating its effectiveness with significantly reduced memory costs and improved recommendation accuracy over the original LATTICE model, a variant of NGCF.

Paper P (DRAGON) directly adopts the training paradigm of Paper Q (BPR): P uses Q’s Bayesian Personalized Ranking loss as its main optimization objective for implicit-feedback recommendation, constructing triplets (u, i, j) where user u has interacted with positive item i but not with negative item j, and maximizing the log-sigmoid of the score difference y_ui − y_uj plus L2 regularization, exactly following the pairwise ranking formulation introduced in Q. In P, this BPR loss is applied on top of DRAGON’s dual user–item representations learned from heterogeneous user–item graphs and homogeneous user–user and item–item graphs, so Q provides the core loss function and learning philosophy for optimizing P’s multimodal graph-based model, rather than serving as an architectural baseline or source of pretrained components.

Paper P (DRAGON) directly builds on Paper Q (LightGCN) by adopting LightGCN’s simplified graph convolution as the backbone on each modality-specific user–item graph: P uses the same symmetric normalized neighborhood aggregation over the interaction graph, sums embeddings from multiple propagation layers as final user/item representations, and optimizes them with the same BPR ranking loss introduced in Q. On top of this LightGCN-style collaborative filtering core, P extends Q to the multimodal setting by initializing item nodes with visual/text features, constructing separate heterogeneous graphs per modality, and then augmenting them with homogeneous user–user co-occurrence and item–item semantic graphs plus an attentive concatenation fusion module. Experimentally, P also includes LightGCN as a key general CF baseline and reports consistent gains, so Q functions both as P’s architectural template for propagation/training and as an important empirical comparison point.

Paper P (DRAGON) builds directly on Paper Q (LATTICE) in both modeling ideas and experimental setup. From Q, P adopts the core insight that multimodal item-item semantic relations, mined from visual/text features and encoded as graphs, can complement user–item interaction graphs for better multimedia recommendation. Concretely, P’s modality-specific item semantic graphs are constructed almost exactly following Q’s KNN-based cosine-similarity scheme (computing modality-wise similarities, keeping top-k neighbors, sparsifying/normalizing the graph), but P drops Q’s learned graph-structure refinement and skip-connection mechanism, instead freezing a simpler binary item graph and combining modalities with fixed weights. On top of Q’s item–item graph idea, P extends the architecture by (1) adding a user–user homogeneous co-occurrence graph and heterogeneous user–item graphs to learn dual user/item representations, and (2) replacing LATTICE’s plug-in CF design with a unified LightGCN-style backbone plus attentive concatenation fusion. Empirically, P also treats Q as a strong multimodal baseline and reports that DRAGON outperforms LATTICE on several Amazon domains, positioning P as a dual-graph generalization and simplification of Q’s latent-structure mining framework rather than a reuse of Q’s trained parameters.

Paper P (DRAGON) treats Paper Q (SLMRec) as an important prior and a strong multimodal baseline rather than something it directly extends: P cites Q in its related work as a representative method that injects self-supervised contrastive tasks (feature dropout/masking and fine–coarse space alignment) into a GNN-based multimedia recommender to mine latent multimodal patterns, while P instead sticks to a purely supervised BPR objective and focuses on enhancing dyadic relations via dual user–item representations learned from heterogeneous user–item graphs and homogeneous user–user and item–item graphs, plus a simple attentive concatenation fusion strategy; in experiments P includes Q as a key comparison model and reports that DRAGON consistently outperforms SLMRec on Amazon Baby, Sports, and Clothing, but it does not reuse Q’s SSL losses, data augmentations, or pretrained parameters, positioning itself as an alternative supervised graph-based architecture inspired by but not built on Q’s training paradigm.

Paper P (MGCN) builds directly on Paper Q (LightGCN) by using LightGCN’s embedding-propagation backbone in its user–item view: it propagates user and item ID embeddings over the normalized user–item graph with the same Laplacian-based update and layer-wise averaging as LightGCN, then applies the same inner-product predictor and BPR-style training; on top of this LightGCN-style collaborative filtering core, P adds its own behavior-guided modality purifier, item–item GCN views, and behavior-aware multimodal fusion, and it also includes LightGCN as a key general CF baseline in its experiments.

Paper P (MGCN) explicitly builds on Paper Q (M2GRL) at the modeling level: inspired by Q’s idea of constructing a separate graph for each view and learning multiple graph-based representations instead of fusing all side information into one vector, P designs a multi-view information encoder that uses a user–item interaction graph to capture collaborative signals and modality-specific item–item KNN graphs to capture semantically correlative signals, citing M2GRL as the template for multi-view graph representation learning. Compared with Q, which aligns instance-, shop-, and category-view graphs via multi-task objectives and uncertainty-based loss weighting for general web-scale recommendation, P adapts this multi-view, multi-graph paradigm to the multimodal recommendation setting (visual/text features) and augments it with a behavior-guided modality purifier, a behavior-aware fusion mechanism, and a contrastive auxiliary loss, while using M2GRL only as a conceptual and architectural foundation rather than as a baseline model or source of pretrained components.

Paper P (MGCN) mainly relates to Paper Q (BM3) by treating BM3 as a strong state-of-the-art multimodal recommendation baseline: P uses the BM3 model, datasets, and MMRec implementation provided by Q to perform fair experimental comparisons, reporting that MGCN consistently outperforms BM3 on Amazon Baby, Sports, and Clothing in Recall and NDCG. Methodologically, P does not reuse BM3’s bootstrap contrastive framework or its negative-sample-free multi-modal contrastive loss; instead, it proposes a different GCN-based multi-view architecture with a behavior-guided purifier and behavior-aware fusion plus its own mutual-information-style auxiliary loss. Thus, the technical relationship from P to Q is primarily comparative and empirical—P positions itself as an improved alternative to Q rather than a direct architectural extension, pretrained component, or training paradigm reuse.

Paper P (LGMRec) relates to Paper Q (BM3) mainly at the level of problem setting and empirical comparison rather than direct architectural reuse. Both tackle multimodal recommendation on the same Amazon Baby/Sports/Clothing benchmarks with visual and textual features and use LightGCN-style collaborative embeddings as a common backbone context. Q proposes BM3 as a self-supervised multimodal model that removes negative sampling and auxiliary graphs via latent-embedding dropout and a multi-modal contrastive loss, while P instead keeps a supervised BPR objective and designs a different architecture: it decouples collaborative and modality-specific embeddings in a local graph embedding module, and adds a global hypergraph embedding module to capture modality-aware global item/user dependencies. In its experiments and discussion, P includes BM3 as one of the strongest prior multimodal baselines and reports consistent improvements over BM3, positioning LGMRec as an alternative local–global graph learning framework that competes with, but does not extend or reuse, BM3’s bootstrap contrastive machinery.

Paper P (LGMRec) builds on Paper Q (SLMRec) mainly at the level of training paradigm and empirical comparison: inspired by Q’s idea of enhancing multimedia recommendation with self-supervised contrastive objectives on top of a graph-based CF backbone, P also introduces an InfoNCE-style contrastive loss, but applies it to cross-modal hypergraph embeddings of users and items to enforce consistency of global modality-aware interests, instead of Q’s feature-level augmentations (FD/FM) and fine–coarse modality-space alignment on item representations; in addition, P treats SLMRec as a strong prior multimodal baseline and reports that LGMRec consistently outperforms SLMRec on the shared Amazon Baby/Sports/Clothing benchmarks in Recall and NDCG, so Q serves both as the self-supervised multimodal recommendation framework that motivates P’s use of contrastive learning and as an important empirical reference point.

Paper P (LGMRec) builds directly on Paper Q (LightGCN) by adopting LightGCN’s simplified graph convolution and layer-combination scheme as its collaborative backbone: in P’s collaborative graph embedding (CGE) and modality graph embedding (MGE) modules, user–item ID embeddings and projected modality features are propagated over the interaction graph using the same symmetrically normalized adjacency D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} and mean aggregation over multiple layers as in LightGCN, and the final user–item scores are trained with the same BPR ranking loss. On top of this LightGCN-style CF core, P extends Q to the multimodal setting by decoupling collaborative and modality-specific local embeddings, introducing a global hypergraph embedding module that models modality-aware attribute hyperedges plus cross-modal InfoNCE contrastive losses, and then fusing local and global representations for prediction, while also using LightGCN as an important non-multimodal baseline in its experimental comparison.

In LGMRec: Local and Global Graph Learning for Multimodal Recommendation (P), the authors cite Revisiting Graph Based Collaborative Filtering: A Linear Residual Graph Convolutional Network Approach (LR-GCCF) (Q) in the related-work discussion of graph-based collaborative filtering as a representative method that simplifies GCN-based CF with linear propagation and residual preference learning; P does not reuse Q’s architecture or experiments directly, but builds on the same line of graph-based CF work by also adopting lightweight GCN-style propagation for collaborative signals and then extending beyond Q to the multimodal setting with decoupled local (collaborative vs. modality) embeddings and a new hypergraph-based global interest module.

P (DA-MRSuses)uses Q (LATTICE)as a key baseline for comparison in its experiments and builds on Q's structure-based multi-modal recommendation paradigm by extending it with denoising mechanisms for multi-modal content and user feedback, and introducing additional alignment techniques to enhance robustness and performance.

Paper P cites Paper Q as a foundational work on denoising implicit feedback in recommender systems and uses Q's proposed Adaptive Denoising Training (ADT) strategies, specifically the Truncated Cross-Entropy (T-CE) loss and Reweighted Cross-Entropy (R-CE) loss, as key baselines for comparative evaluation. In Section 4.2.2 of P, the authors explicitly compare their DA-MRS framework against T-CE and R-CE from Q, demonstrating that DA-MRS achieves superior performance by leveraging multi-modal content and alignment techniques, whereas Q's methods are limited to loss-based denoising without multi-modal integration. This relationship highlights how P builds on Q by addressing its limitations in handling multi-modal noise and feedback, while using Q's established denoising approaches as benchmarks to validate the effectiveness of P's novel contributions.

Paper P(DA-MRS) uses Paper Q(SGDL) as an important baseline for comparison in its experiments on denoising recommender systems, citing SGDL in the related work and attempting to evaluate against it, though technical issues prevented direct comparison. P builds on the general idea of denoising user feedback from Q but extends it to multi-modal settings by incorporating denoising of multi-modal content and introducing alignment techniques, rather than directly adopting Q's self-guided learning paradigm.

P(SMORE) uses Q(MGCN) as a key baseline for comparison in its experiments, as shown in Table 2 of P, where MGCN (Q) is evaluated alongside other state-of-the-art methods. P builds on Q's approach to modality noise reduction by adopting a similar behavior-guided purification mechanism (e.g., Equations 12–13 in P mirror Equation 2 in Q) but extends it significantly through spectrum-based fusion in the frequency domain. Specifically, P introduces Fourier transforms and dynamic filtering to attenuate cross-modality noise during fusion, whereas Q operates solely in the spatial domain with multi-view encoding. P also incorporates a modality-aware preference module that balances uni-modal and fused features, refining Q's behavior-aware fuser by leveraging fusion features to weigh uni-modal attention.

P (SMORE)uses Q (FREEDOM)as an important baseline for comparison in its experiments, as shown in Table 2 of P, where Q (cited as FREEDOM [50]) is evaluated alongside other state-of-the-art multimodal recommenders. P builds on the multimodal recommendation paradigm by addressing modality noise, a concern also highlighted in Q, but introduces a novel spectrum-based fusion approach in the frequency domain for denoising, whereas Q employs graph freezing and degree-sensitive edge pruning. P demonstrates superior performance over Q, indicating an advancement in handling cross-modality noise and fusion efficiency.

Paper P (SMORE) builds directly on the frequency domain fusion and denoising techniques introduced in Paper Q (FSRU). Specifically, P adopts Q's core idea of using Fourier transforms to project multimodal features into the frequency domain for efficient and discriminative representation learning. P extends Q's approach by integrating it into a graph convolutional network for multimodal recommendation, whereas Q focused on rumor detection. P cites Q as inspiration for leveraging the sparse and global properties of the frequency spectrum to attenuate modality-specific noise during fusion, and further enhances this with adaptive dynamic filters and graph-based semantic correlation learning tailored to recommendation tasks.

Paper P (SMORE) builds directly on Paper Q (LightGCN) by adopting its simplified graph convolution architecture for multimodal recommendation. Specifically, P is inspired by LightGCN's efficacy and simplicity in neighborhood aggregation without feature transformation or nonlinear activation. P extends LightGCN's light graph convolution layer to propagate both uni-modal and fusion features in its multi-modal graph learning module, using a similar propagation rule (e.g., symmetric normalization and shallow layers). Additionally, P uses LightGCN as a key baseline for comparison in experiments, demonstrating improvements over it in multimodal settings.

Paper P(PGL) uses Paper Q (LGMRec) as an important baseline for experimental comparison and performance evaluation. In Table 1 of P, LGMRec is included as a state-of-the-art multimodal recommendation method, and PGL is shown to outperform it across multiple datasets. Additionally, P discusses Q in its related work section, acknowledging that LGMRec designs hypergraph networks to mine both global and local structural features, but criticizes it for still over-emphasizing co-occurrence patterns and neglecting individual information. This critique motivates P to propose the PGL framework, which focuses on extracting principal subgraphs to better capture local structural features and individual information, thereby addressing the limitation identified in Q.

Paper P(PGL) uses Paper Q (MGCN) as an important baseline for experimental comparison and performance evaluation. In Table 1 of P, MGCN is included as a state-of-the-art multimedia recommendation method, and PGL is shown to outperform it across multiple datasets. Additionally, P discusses Q in its related work section, acknowledging that MGCN adds a modality noise filter to remove preference-irrelevant noise but criticizes it for still focusing on global structural features and underutilizing individual information. This critique motivates P to propose the PGL framework, which addresses this limitation by extracting principal subgraphs to better capture local structural features and individual information. P also includes MGCN in its efficiency comparison (Table 2) to highlight PGL's competitive training time and memory usage.

P builds on Q's lightweight graph convolution (LightGCN) by adopting its parameter-free linear message passing mechanism as a core component for embedding propagation. P extends Q's architecture by introducing principal subgraph extraction (via global-aware and local-aware operators) to capture local structural features, addressing Q's limitation in underutilizing individual information. Additionally, P uses Q as a key baseline in experimental comparisons to demonstrate the superiority of PGL in recommendation performance.

Paper P adopts the self-supervised learning paradigm of Q by adding an auxiliary InfoNCE-based contrastive loss with feature masking, directly inspired by Q’s node-level self-discrimination framework. While Q introduces self-supervised graph learning (SGL) to enhance robustness and representation quality, P extends this idea into the multimedia recommendation setting by integrating a similar self-supervised objective into its Principal Graph Learning framework. In addition, P treats Q as an important baseline for comparison, reporting results against SGL to demonstrate improvements.

Paper P (MVGAE) builds directly on Paper Q’s (Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes / VAE) variational learning paradigm: it models each node embedding as a Gaussian latent variable inferred by an encoder and trained by maximizing an ELBO consisting of a reconstruction term plus a KL regularizer, and it uses Q’s reparameterization trick (sampling via z = μ + σ ⊙ ε) to backpropagate through stochastic latent sampling during training. On top of Q’s generic VAE framework, P extends the encoder/decoder design to a graph setting (GCN-based variational encoders and an interaction reconstruction objective for user–item links) and further introduces a multi-modal posterior fusion mechanism (product-of-experts) to combine modality-specific Gaussian posteriors within the same VAE/ELBO framework.

Paper P (MVGAE) borrows the core GCN idea from Paper Q: using graph convolution/message-passing neighborhood aggregation on an adjacency-defined graph to propagate and mix node features so that node embeddings capture both graph structure and features. In MVGAE, these GCN-based layers serve as the backbone of its modality-specific encoders and the collaborative encoder, taking the user–item adjacency matrix (with self-loops) plus node features as input and producing node representations used to infer latent variables. MVGAE then extends beyond Q by outputting variational Gaussian parameters (mean/variance) from these GCN encoders and using them for VAE-style training and multi-modal fusion (PoE), while Q’s original objective is semi-supervised node classification with cross-entropy.

P (DualGNN) directly borrows Q’s training objective: it optimizes user–item rankings with the Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR) pairwise loss by sampling training triplets (u, i, j) where i is an observed (positive) micro-video and j is an unobserved (negative) one, and minimizing a sigmoid-based loss on the score difference (y_{u,i} − y_{u,j}) with L2 regularization. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0} This matches Q’s core idea of optimizing personalized ranking via a log-sigmoid likelihood on pairwise score differences (i.e., ln σ( x̂_{uij} )) plus regularization.

DualGNN builds on LightGCN mainly by borrowing its “light graph convolution + layer combination” design for collaborative filtering: in DualGNN’s single-modal representation learning, it explicitly removes self-loop propagation and feature transformation, and uses symmetric-normalized neighbor aggregation as the propagation rule :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}, which matches LightGCN’s core simplification that keeps only normalized neighbor aggregation while removing self-connection/feature transformation/nonlinearity. DualGNN also follows LightGCN’s idea of combining multi-layer embeddings by summing/aggregating representations from all propagation layers to form final node embeddings, corresponding to LightGCN’s layer-combination (weighted-sum) final embedding formulation. Concretely, DualGNN applies this LightGCN-style propagation independently on each modality-specific user–item bipartite graph to obtain per-modality user/item representations, and then extends beyond LightGCN by adding its own multimodal construction/aggregation (e.g., user co-occurrence graph + attentive fusion) rather than relying only on ID-based interaction propagation. Additionally, DualGNN uses LightGCN as a key baseline in experiments and discusses it explicitly as a strong GCN-based CF method.
